connector: Last time, the children stood in a sad, quiet ruin with walls all around. Today it gets a name. Watch Peter lay out his clues one by one, the way a good mender checks each page before saying what a book is. Then follow the torch down sixteen steps into the dark.

a.raw: susan found her presents the bow the ivory quiver and the feathered arrows
a.fixed: Susan found her presents — the bow, the ivory quiver, and the feathered arrows.
a.why: Capital S on Susan; a dash before the list for emphasis; commas between the three presents; a period ends it.

b.raw: lucy took down her gift the little diamond bottle of cordial
b.fixed: Lucy took down her gift — the little diamond bottle of cordial.
b.why: Capital L on Lucy; a dash points to the gift and makes the reader look at it; a period ends it.

notes.wgrd: Watch the children’s understanding of the place change. Each new clue (the chess-knight, the well, the orchard, the hidden door) moves them closer to knowing where they are.
vocab: A place where things meet or connect, especially where train lines split.
A dense group of bushes or small trees growing closely together.
Thorny bushes, especially wild blackberry or raspberry bushes with prickly stems.
Lived in; having people or creatures living there.
notes.wordParts: Prefixes: pre- = before, re- = again or back, trans- = across, inter- = between: preview, return, transport, international.
notes.grammar: Conjunctions join ideas. And adds one idea to another; or offers a choice between them. Stay in the castle or ride into the woods means one, not both. Lewis uses or when only one thing can be true.
notes.spelling: To split a long word, peel off the prefix and suffix first, then the base is easy: un + familiar, transport + ed, discover + ed.

virtue.title: Which pillar is it?
virtue.intro: In Chapter 2 the children find their old treasure chamber. Read each moment. Tap the pillar it shows best.

items.t: Lucy asks where Susan’s horn is. Susan thinks, then says she took it hunting on their last day in Narnia and must have lost it.
items.why: Susan tells the truth about losing something very important.

items.t: In the middle of the treasures, Edmund says, “We mustn’t waste the battery.” They take what they need and go.
items.why: Edmund remembers they will need the torch again.

items.t: Peter’s pocket-knife breaks while they clear the ivy from the hidden door. They keep going with Edmund’s.
items.why: They don’t quit when the tool breaks.
items.hint: What happens after the knife breaks?

items.t: Edmund goes first down the dark steps with the light, counting them out loud.
items.why: He leads the way into a place none of them can see.
items.hint: Who goes first into the dark?

transcripts.welcome: Hello again, it’s Nell. Yesterday the children found a quiet, sad ruin. Today they find out whose it was. Today’s question: what new details do you learn about this place, and how does the children’s understanding of it change?
transcripts.read: Watch Peter work it out one point at a time: the hall, the well, a little golden chess piece, an orchard. Then a hollow sound behind the ivy. When they go down the steps, count with them. And notice which gift isn’t where it should be.
transcripts.grammar: And and or are small words with big jobs. And says both things are true. Or says choose one. The bread and the cheese means you get both. The bread or the cheese means you get one. When you see or, ask: what is the choice?
